extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic / philosophy of language
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter-level analysis classifying kinds of linguistic names/terms (syncategorematic vs categorematic, general vs singular, concrete vs abstract, connotative vs non-connotative, many-worded names, etc.) and explaining their role in propositions. Intended to guide analysis of propositions by first analysing the meanings and functions of names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-names / parts of names (syncategorematic terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words that are not names but only parts of names (particles, some inflected cases, and certain words like adverbs) and therefore cannot by themselves be subjects or predicates of propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: of, to, truly, me, him, John's; adjectives like large or heavy (when not used to denote a whole object) are not names in this sense. Such words do not express things of which anything can be affirmed or denied (e.g., 'Truly' cannot stand alone as 'Truly was asserted'). Exception: they may be full names when we speak of the mere words themselves (suppositio materialis). Schoolmen called these syncategorematic; they contrast with categorematic terms which can be used alone as subject or predicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorematic terms (words usable as names alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words which can be used either as the subject or predicate of a proposition without being accompanied by any other word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A categorematic term can stand alone (e.g., snow, white as predicate in 'Snow is white'). Mixed terms (several words forming a single name) are, in the useful sense, categorematic. This distinction is largely grammatical/logical and helps determine which expressions can function as complete terms in propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-worded names / testing whether a phrase is one name
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of words that together constitute a single name (one categorematic term) rather than multiple names; determined by whether predicating of the expression yields one assertion or several.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: predicate something of the phrase and observe whether you make one assertion or several. Examples: the long phrase from Paradise Lost counts as one name for a logician; 'John Nokes, who was the mayor of the town, died yesterday' makes one assertion about that whole phrase, showing it is a single name. Contrast with 'John Nokes and the mayor of the town died yesterday' which makes two assertions and therefore denotes two names.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names (names of a class) vs Individual (singular) names
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is capable of being truly affirmed, in the same sense, of an indefinite number of things; an individual or singular name can only be truly affirmed (in the same sense) of one thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'man' can be affirmed of John, Peter, George etc. in the same sense — thus a general name; 'John' is only predicable (in the same sense) of one person and is a singular name. 'The present king of England' is an individual name by meaning. The author notes that stating a general name is essentially naming a class, and suggests defining 'class' via the general name rather than vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective names vs general names
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective names denote a multitude taken together and cannot be predicated of each member separately, whereas general names can be predicated of each individual of a multitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the 76th regiment of foot' is a collective name (not general) because it applies to the regiment as a whole and not to each soldier separately; 'a regiment' is both collective and general (general across regiments, collective with respect to soldiers within a regiment). This distinction matters for correct predication of statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete names vs Abstract names
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete names stand for things (objects); abstract names stand for attributes (qualities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: John, the sea, this table are concrete; 'white' as used to predicate is a name of objects having the quality, while 'whiteness' is the name of the attribute itself. The author uses the classical schoolmen sense (abstract = name of attribute) and warns about a modern practice that misapplies 'abstract' to all general names. The distinction affects what is being denied or affirmed in propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives as names and grammatical ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives can serve as predicates and, occasionally, as subjects (the latter often explained by ellipsis) and therefore can function as names in logical analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Snow is white' (adjective as predicate); occasionally 'White is an agreeable colour' (ellipsis for 'a white colour'). Some languages (Greek, Latin) permit broader ellipsis than English. For logical purposes the adjective can be treated as a name (either standing for the quality or for objects having the quality) depending on principal use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative vs Non-connotative (absolute) terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-connotative term signifies a subject only, or an attribute only; a connotative term denotes a subject and implies (connote) an attribute of that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Proper names like John or London are non-connotative (signify subject only); 'whiteness', 'length', 'virtue' signify attributes only (non-connotative). Words like 'white', 'long', 'virtuous' denote subjects (snow, men, etc.) and connote the attributes (whiteness, length, virtue). All concrete general names are connotative because they denote subjects by virtue of attributes they imply. Connotation is the attribute-content that gives meaningful information when the name is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names (as non-connotative) and their independence from attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names are attached to objects and do not imply attributes; they serve as mere marks to identify individuals and strictly have no signification (no connotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mary, Caesar; although there may have been reasons for choosing a name (named after a father or a place), once given the name becomes independent of that reason. If the spatiotemporal fact that motivated the name ceases (e.g., river mouth moves), the proper name need not change — showing the name does not connote that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative individual names / ways an individual name may connote attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual names may nonetheless be connotative when the name itself (or its context) implies an attribute that uniquely picks out one individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: (1) the meaning of the name may include uniqueness (e.g., 'the only son of John Stiles'); (2) the attribute connoted may be a connection with a determinate event so that, in fact, only one individual had that connection ('the murderer of Henri Quatre'); (3) a many-worded general name limited by context or adjuncts may become individual ('the present prime minister of England' — 'present' limits it to one person at a time). These show how connotation + limiting words or context can individualize an expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological principle: analyze names before analyzing propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because every proposition consists of two names and affirmation/denial concerns what the names are names of, the meaning of names and their relation to things must be the preliminary stage of analyzing propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: To analyze propositions further one is forced to consider the import of names; starting from names brings before us distinctions recognised by ordinary language and the collective intelligence of mankind. An enumeration/classification of things not starting from names risks omitting distinctions established by language. Thus, study of names is necessary and practical prior to deeper analysis of propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signification resides in connotation rather than mere denotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the names given to objects convey information (have signification), that meaning resides not in what they denote (the subjects) but in what they connote (the attributes implied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Proper names are the only names that connote nothing and thus have no real signification. For other names the informative content — what we tell about an individual when we use the name — comes from the connotation (the attributes) rather than simple denotation of the object named.
